chunks: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Qattan narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Zakariya al-Qattan narrated to us, saying: Bakr ibn Abdullah ibn Habib narrated to us, saying: Tamim ibn Buhlool narrated to us, saying: Abdul Rahman ibn al-Aswad narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Abdul Rahman ibn Mu'amir, from Ammar ibn Yasir, and from Jabir ibn Abdullah, that they said:

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said to Ali (peace be upon him): 'I shall reason with you on the Day of Resurrection, reasoning with you based on Prophethood, and you shall reason with your people, reasoning with them based on seven characteristics: establishment of prayer, payment of alms-tax, enjoining good, forbidding evil, justice among the subjects, fair division, and carrying out the command of God, the Mighty and Exalted. Do you not know, O Ali, that Abraham (peace be upon him) will be with us on the Day of Resurrection? He will be called and placed on the right side of the Throne, dressed in the attire of Paradise, adorned with its ornaments, and a gutter of gold will flow for him from Paradise, from which he will pour what is sweeter than honey, whiter than milk, and colder than snow. Then I will be called and placed on the left side of the Throne, and the same will be done to me. Then you, O Ali, will be called and the same will be done to you. Do you not like, O Ali, that you are called when I am called, dressed when I am dressed, and adorned when I am adorned? Indeed, God, the Mighty and Exalted, commanded me to bring you close so I do not distance you, and to teach you so I do not neglect you. It is incumbent upon you to learn, and it is incumbent upon me to obey my Lord, the Blessed and Exalted.'
ai.seo_question: What are the seven characteristics by which Ali will reason with people on the Day of Resurrection according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Khisal highlights the eschatological precedence of Ali (AS), illustrating his unique status through the 'seven characteristics' by which he will evaluate humanity, mirroring the Prophet's own role. The narrative emphasizes the concept of *Munajat* (intimate dialogue) and shared divine honor, where Abraham, the Prophet, and Ali are depicted as receiving parallel accolades near the Throne, underscoring Ali's integral role in the cosmic order of judgment. This reflects the Shia scholarly understanding of Ali as the perfect executor of divine command, whose authority is inextricably linked to the Prophet's own spiritual and temporal legacy.
